title: One Will or Two? How an NRI Should Structure a Will Covering Assets in India and Abroad
subtitle: An NRI with a flat in Kolkata and a brokerage account in New Jersey is really managing two different legal systems at once, and the will that works perfectly for one can quietly destroy the other.
seo_title: NRI Wills: One Will or Two for India & Abroad
meta_description: Why an NRI with assets in India and abroad usually needs two linked wills, and how a careless revocation clause can cancel the Indian will entirely.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian
standfirst: An NRI who owns a flat or ancestral home in India and a house, retirement account or brokerage portfolio abroad is not dealing with one estate, legally speaking, but two, governed by different rules that can conflict with each other in ways a single, well-meaning will often fails to anticipate. The question that follows from this, whether to write one will covering everything or two separate wills tied to each jurisdiction, is not a matter of personal preference. It is a question with a right answer in most cases, and getting it wrong can mean the later will someone signs abroad accidentally cancels the Indian will they thought was still standing.
key_points: Section 5 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925 splits succession along asset type: immovable property is governed by the law of the country where it is situated, regardless of the owner's domicile, while movable property follows the law of the owner's domicile at death

Domicile is a legal concept distinct from residence or citizenship, and under Sections 6 to 13 of the Act it does not change merely because an NRI has lived abroad for years on a work visa; it requires an actual intention to make that country a permanent home

Most cross-border estate planners recommend two linked wills rather than one, an India-specific will for Indian assets and a separate will for foreign assets, because each can be drafted to match the formalities and probate expectations of its own jurisdiction

The single most common way an NRI's Indian will gets destroyed by accident is a later foreign will containing a standard, broad revocation clause that cancels all prior wills everywhere, not just the one it was meant to replace

Section 70 of the Indian Succession Act allows revocation only by specific modes, a later will or codicil, a written declaration of intent to revoke, or physical destruction with that intention, and the Supreme Court has held an agreement cannot do what Section 70 requires

Section 69 automatically revokes a will on the testator's later marriage, but only for Christians, Parsis and Jews; wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, Jains and Muslims are not revoked by marriage at all, a distinction the Kerala High Court upheld as constitutional on 8 October 2026

Where a will has already been probated abroad, Section 228 lets an Indian court grant ancillary administration on the strength of that foreign probate rather than requiring a fresh probate petition to prove the will all over again, though the procedure still needs to go through an Indian court

Naming different executors for the Indian and foreign wills, someone who can actually act in each country without needing a power of attorney or visa to do so, avoids the single most common practical delay in administering a cross-border estate

sections.heading: Why This Question Comes Up for Almost Every NRI With Property in Two Countries
paragraphs: Most NRIs who sit down to write a will start from the instinct that one document, covering everything they own anywhere in the world, is simpler and therefore safer. For a person whose entire estate sits in one country, that instinct is usually right. For an NRI with a flat or ancestral property in India and a house, a retirement account or a brokerage portfolio in the country where they now live, it is usually wrong, because the two halves of that estate are not actually governed by the same legal system, and a document drafted to satisfy one country's formalities can fail, or worse, backfire, when read against the other's.

This is not a hypothetical risk confined to unusual cases. It arises for any NRI who owns Indian immovable property, a home, agricultural land inherited from parents, a flat bought before emigrating, alongside assets built up abroad over a working life, a pension, a 401(k) or equivalent, a house, shares held through a foreign broker. The question of one will or two is, in substance, a question about which country's court will be asked to act on which part of the will, and whether the way the will is written helps or hinders that court when the time comes.

The stakes are highest for families where the assets on each side are substantial enough that a mistake is expensive to unwind, and where the testator's own later life, remarriage, estrangement from one branch of the family, or simply the passage of years between drafting an Indian will and later updating an estate plan abroad, creates the conditions for a gap or a conflict between the two halves of the estate to go unnoticed until it is too late to fix.

It is also worth being clear about what this article does not cover. It assumes the testator already has a functioning Indian will, or is about to make one, and is asking how that will should sit alongside a separate estate plan abroad. It does not repeat the mechanics of Indian probate, succession certificates, or the FEMA limits on repatriating sale proceeds once an estate is actually being administered, which a separate guide on this site addresses in full. The questions here are upstream of all of that: how many documents to execute, what each should say about the other, and which legal system actually governs which half of the estate before any dispute or any probate petition has even begun.

sections.heading: The Conflict-of-Laws Split: Lex Situs for Immovables, Domicile for Movables
paragraphs: The starting point for understanding why a single will can go wrong is Section 5 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, which splits succession along the line of asset type rather than nationality or residence. Succession to immovable property follows the law of the country where that property is situated, a rule private international lawyers call lex situs, regardless of where the owner was domiciled or where they died. Succession to movable property, by contrast, follows the law of the country where the deceased was domiciled at the time of death, under Section 5(2). Section 19 supplies a fallback: in the absence of proof of a different domicile, movable property succession is governed by Indian law.

The practical effect for an NRI is that a flat in India is governed by Indian succession law no matter how long the owner has lived abroad or which country's passport they carry, while a bank account, a brokerage portfolio or a retirement fund held abroad can be governed by the law of the NRI's actual domicile, which, for someone genuinely settled abroad for the long term, is very often that foreign country rather than India. A single estate can therefore be split between two legal regimes the moment it crosses the immovable-movable line, and a will drafted with only one of those regimes in mind risks getting the other one wrong.

Immovable property situated in a third country, say an NRI who owns a flat in Dubai in addition to property in India and a home in the country of residence, follows the law of wherever that third property is located, which can mean a single testator's estate is, in the fullest case, governed by three separate legal systems rather than two. Each additional jurisdiction adds another set of local formality rules the will has to satisfy if it is to be given effect there without a fight.

The distinction between movable and immovable property is itself not always as obvious as it sounds, and this is where families sometimes get the split wrong without realising it. Shares in an Indian company are movable property under Section 44 of the Companies Act, 2013, even though the underlying business may hold Indian land or run an Indian factory, so a shareholding, unlike a flat, is a candidate for being governed by the testator's domicile rather than automatically by Indian law merely because the company is Indian and the shares sit in an Indian demat account. How cleanly that domicile rule actually applies once shares are held in dematerialised form, where the depository participant and the registered owner are not the same person, is less settled than the rule for a plain shareholding, and commentary on the point does not fully agree, so an NRI with a significant demat holding should treat its classification as a question for the will drafter to confirm specifically rather than assume it follows the same path as the family home.

sections.heading: Domicile Is Not Residence, and It Rarely Changes by Accident
paragraphs: A great deal of confusion in this area comes from treating domicile as a simple function of where someone currently lives or works. Indian law treats it as a more demanding concept. Sections 7 and 8 fix a person's domicile of origin, generally tied to their father's domicile at birth, and Sections 10 to 13 govern how a domicile of choice can replace it, which requires both actual residence in the new country and a genuine, settled intention to make it a permanent home, not merely a convenient one for as long as work or circumstances require.

This matters enormously for an NRI who has lived abroad for a decade or more on a long-term visa, a green card, or even citizenship, but who has always planned, or at least kept open the possibility, of eventually returning to India. Secondary commentary consistently makes the point that years of foreign residence taken on its own, without more, does not establish a change of domicile; residence taken up for employment, however long it lasts, is not by itself proof of an intention to abandon the domicile of origin permanently. The presumption runs against a change of domicile, and the burden of showing one has occurred sits with whoever asserts it.

An NRI's own uncertainty about where they will eventually settle is, in a sense, exactly the condition that keeps their domicile anchored to India under this framework, which is a useful thing to know when deciding how to structure the will. A testator whose domicile is still India can find that even assets held abroad fall to be distributed, as far as succession law is concerned, according to Indian rules rather than the foreign country's own succession regime, a result that surprises many families who assumed the opposite simply because the asset itself sits overseas. Confirming the actual domicile position, rather than assuming it from citizenship or years abroad, is accordingly one of the first things worth settling before deciding how many wills to write and what each should say.

Domicile can also change more than once over a working life, and each change carries its own evidentiary burden. An NRI who acquired a genuine domicile of choice abroad, say by taking citizenship, buying a permanent home, and severing most ties to India, can later regain an Indian domicile under Section 11 by returning with the settled intention of staying, even without formally giving up the foreign citizenship first. A family that assumes domicile is fixed once acquired, rather than something that can shift again with a later change in intention and residence, risks drafting both wills around a domicile position that no longer matches the testator's actual circumstances by the time either document is needed.

sections.heading: The Case for Separate, Situs-Specific Wills
paragraphs: Cross-border estate planners, in India and in the common destination countries for Indian emigrants alike, consistently recommend two linked wills over one combined document: an India-specific will dealing only with Indian assets, executed in the form Indian courts expect, and a separate will for the foreign assets, executed to satisfy the formalities of the country where the testator is domiciled or where those assets sit. The reasoning is practical rather than theoretical. A will intended to be probated in India has to satisfy Indian courts and Indian registries that it is genuine and was properly executed; a will intended to be probated abroad has to satisfy a different court applying different formality rules, and a single document asked to do both jobs at once tends to do neither cleanly.

A foreign probate order, obtained in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada or elsewhere, does not automatically take effect over Indian assets. Indian succession to Indian immovable property remains governed by Indian law under Section 5, and an Indian court or registry dealing with Indian property will look to Indian probate or a comparable Indian instrument, not to a foreign court's order standing alone, before recognising a transfer. Relying on a single foreign will to carry an Indian flat through Indian succession, without any Indian-facing document or process, routinely produces delay precisely because the Indian institutions involved, land registries, banks, housing societies, are simply not set up to act on a foreign court's paper without more.

The reverse is equally true. An Indian-style will, drafted with Indian witnessing and attestation conventions in mind, can create unnecessary friction when presented to a foreign probate court that expects its own jurisdiction's formalities, such as a self-proving affidavit common in many American states, even where the Indian will would otherwise be perfectly valid there. Separate, situs-specific wills let each document be built around what the relevant court will actually expect to see, rather than asking one document to anticipate two, or three, different sets of expectations at once.

There is also a practical speed argument for separate wills that families often underestimate until they are living through a slow administration. A will confined to Indian assets is a simpler, shorter document for an Indian probate court to work through than a lengthy foreign-style will that spends most of its pages on a trust, a retirement account or a foreign business interest an Indian court has no reason to concern itself with at all. Keeping the Indian will narrowly focused on Indian assets, and leaving everything else to the foreign will, tends to shorten the time an Indian court needs to satisfy itself the document is genuine and should be acted upon, simply because there is less in it for anyone to object to or for the court to puzzle over.

sections.heading: The Revocation Trap: How a Later Foreign Will Can Cancel the Indian One by Accident
paragraphs: The single most commonly reported way an NRI's carefully prepared Indian will gets destroyed is not a dispute over its validity, but a standard clause in a later will executed abroad. Most will templates used in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and elsewhere open with a boilerplate recital along the lines of "I hereby revoke all wills and testamentary dispositions heretofore made by me", intended simply to clear away earlier drafts of the same foreign will. Read literally, and without a carve-out, that sentence revokes the Indian will too, even though nobody involved in drafting the foreign will had any intention of touching the Indian estate at all.

Section 70 of the Indian Succession Act governs when and how an earlier will can actually be revoked, and the Supreme Court has read it strictly: revocation can occur only through one of the specific modes the section lists, a later will or codicil, a written declaration of an intention to revoke, or destruction carried out with that intention, and not through any other mechanism, including an agreement between parties that purports to achieve the same result. A later will squarely falls within that list of valid modes, which is exactly why a broad, unqualified revocation clause in a foreign will is legally effective to revoke an earlier Indian will, not a mere technicality that a court will overlook because the drafter probably did not mean it that way.

The fix recommended consistently across cross-border estate planning commentary is to scope each will's revocation clause to the jurisdiction and assets it actually covers: the Indian will should state plainly that it revokes only prior wills dealing with the testator's assets situated in India, and the foreign will should carry the mirror-image limitation, revoking only prior wills dealing with the assets it covers, each expressly stating that it does not revoke or affect the other. This is not a clause either lawyer is likely to insert unprompted if they only see their own half of the estate, which is why having the Indian lawyer and the foreign lawyer actually review each other's draft, rather than working in isolation, is the step most often skipped and most often responsible for the problem surfacing only after the testator has died and it is too late to fix.

The risk runs in both directions, and families sometimes focus only on protecting the Indian will while leaving the foreign will exposed to the same mistake in reverse. An Indian will drafted or updated later in life, using a standard Indian template that opens with an equally broad revocation recital, can just as easily cancel a foreign will that was carefully structured around a trust, a beneficiary designation, or a jurisdiction-specific tax plan the family spent real money setting up. The scoping discipline has to apply symmetrically to both documents, regardless of which one happens to be drafted second, since either will can end up being the later one depending on how an estate plan is updated over the years.

A testator who updates only one will after a life event, the birth of a grandchild, a falling-out with a beneficiary, a change in which charity the family wants to support, should treat that update as an occasion to re-check the other will's scope clause as well, rather than assuming the untouched will remains safely insulated simply because nobody touched it directly. Revocation risk in a cross-border estate plan is a property of how the two documents interact, not a one-time box to tick when they are first signed.

sections.heading: When Marriage Alone Revokes a Will, Whether or Not Anyone Meant It To
paragraphs: A separate revocation trap, unrelated to anything either lawyer drafts, arises from Section 69 of the Indian Succession Act, which provides that a will is revoked automatically by the testator's marriage occurring after it was made. This rule, unlike Section 70, requires no later document and no deliberate act by the testator at all; the marriage itself does the revoking. For an NRI who executed a will before a second marriage, whether following widowhood, divorce, or an earlier marriage that was itself void, this can mean a carefully drafted Indian will is legally dead the moment the wedding takes place, regardless of whether the testator or anyone else realised it.

Section 69 does not apply uniformly across religious communities. It governs wills made by Christians, Parsis and Jews, but has no application to wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs or Jains, which Section 69's own terms exclude, and Muslims fall outside the provision entirely because Section 58 removes testamentary succession for Muslims from the Act's scope altogether, leaving it to Muslim personal law instead. An NRI's personal religious law therefore determines whether remarriage is a drafting event that needs a fresh will immediately, or simply an occasion worth updating the will for in the ordinary course.

The Kerala High Court, sitting on a suo motu reference and reported at 2026:KER:77525, upheld Section 69's constitutional validity on 8 October 2026, rejecting the argument that treating Christian, Parsi and Jewish wills differently from Hindu and Muslim wills on this point amounts to unequal treatment under the Constitution. The ruling leaves the religion-based distinction intact for now, and an NRI belonging to one of the communities Section 69 covers who remarries after making a will should treat the earlier will as revoked in full, not merely in need of an update, until a fresh will is executed.

sections.heading: Matching Each Will to the Witnessing Rules That Will Actually Prove It
paragraphs: Section 63 of the Indian Succession Act requires a will to be signed by the testator and attested by at least two witnesses, each of whom either saw the testator sign or received a personal acknowledgment of the signature, and each of whom signed in the testator's presence. Proving that this happened, when the will is eventually put to probate, generally requires calling at least one of those attesting witnesses to give evidence, a requirement Indian courts enforce strictly regardless of whether the will is actually being contested by anyone.

Most American states have broadly comparable witnessing rules, typically two witnesses, but add a procedural convenience Indian law has no direct equivalent for: a self-proving affidavit, signed by the testator and the witnesses before a notary at the time of execution, which lets many American probate courts admit the will without requiring the witnesses to appear and testify later. An India-facing will gets no benefit from this affidavit, since Indian probate practice still looks to Section 63 read with the attesting-witness requirement in the evidence law rather than to a notarised affidavit, which is one more reason a single document asked to serve both systems ends up optimised for neither.

The practical consequence for drafting is straightforward even if it is often missed: witnesses chosen for the Indian will should be people who are likely to remain reachable and willing to give evidence in an Indian court years later, which argues against using witnesses who are only visiting India briefly or who plan to emigrate themselves soon after the signing. The foreign will's witnesses face a different test, satisfying that jurisdiction's own formality and self-proving requirements, and the two wills should be executed with each jurisdiction's own expectations in mind rather than borrowing one set of witnesses or one execution ceremony for both documents simply for convenience.

A family that signs both wills on the same visit to India, intending the foreign will to be executed later once the testator returns abroad, should resist the temptation to use the same two people as witnesses for both documents purely because they happen to be present. A witness to the Indian will does not need to meet the foreign jurisdiction's own competency or residency expectations for witnessing that country's will, and a witness who is not ordinarily resident in, or even unfamiliar with, the foreign jurisdiction's formality conventions can end up being a weaker witness there than someone chosen specifically with that jurisdiction's probate court in mind. Treating each signing as its own event, with its own appropriate witnesses, costs little in practice and avoids a foreign probate court questioning why a witness unfamiliar with local formality expectations was used for a will meant to be proved there.

sections.heading: If a Will Is Already Probated Abroad: Section 228 and Ancillary Administration
paragraphs: Where an NRI's will has already gone through probate in a foreign court, commentary on Section 228 of the Indian Succession Act describes it as allowing an Indian court to grant administration on the strength of an authenticated copy of a will already proved and a grant already made by a competent court outside India, rather than requiring the executor to prove the will's execution from scratch before an Indian court as though no foreign proceeding had ever happened. This is generally referred to as ancillary administration, and Indian courts have treated a foreign grant obtained this way, once supplemented by the Section 228 process, as carrying the same judgment-in-rem effect a domestic probate would.

This route still requires an application to an Indian court; it is not a mechanism for simply recording a foreign probate in India without any Indian court involvement at all, and whether a particular foreign court's grant qualifies for the simplified Section 228 route, as opposed to requiring an entirely fresh Indian probate petition, can depend on specifics this article has not been able to confirm from a primary source, including which countries' courts the relevant notification or practice actually covers. An NRI whose will has already been probated abroad, or who is structuring a will with this route in mind, should confirm the current position for the specific foreign jurisdiction involved with Indian counsel before assuming the ancillary route will apply automatically.

What Section 228 does make clear, in combination with the general rule under Section 5, is that a foreign probate order is not a substitute for engaging with the Indian legal system over Indian assets; it is, at most, an input into an Indian court process that still has to run its course. An NRI who structures their estate expecting the foreign probate alone to carry Indian property through succession is relying on a shortcut Indian law does not actually provide, and the delay involved in discovering that the shortcut does not exist tends to fall on the family at exactly the time they can least afford to spend months starting an Indian proceeding they assumed had already been taken care of abroad.

sections.heading: Choosing Executors Who Can Actually Act in Each Country
paragraphs: An executor named in a will has to do more than simply be trusted by the testator; they have to be practically able to deal with the courts, banks and registries in the country where that will's assets sit, within a reasonable time and without needing a visa, a power of attorney, or a long-distance flight for every signature. Naming the same person as executor of both the Indian and the foreign will can work where that person genuinely moves between both countries with ease, but it more often creates a bottleneck, particularly where the executor lives abroad and has to act on Indian matters, citations, court appearances, registration formalities, that are easier handled by someone physically present in India.

A common and workable structure is to name a different executor for each will, someone resident in India for the Indian will and someone resident in the country of domicile for the foreign will, with each executor empowered to act independently on their own half of the estate rather than needing the other's sign-off for routine steps. Where family relationships make a single trusted executor the only realistic choice, that executor should at minimum be given a clear power of attorney covering the other jurisdiction's administrative steps, and should understand in advance that administering a cross-border estate single-handedly takes considerably longer than administering either half alone.

Coordination between the two executors, so that one does not take a step, selling an asset, making a distribution, filing a tax return, that affects the other half of the estate without the other knowing, matters more in cross-border administration than in a single-jurisdiction estate, since tax consequences in one country can depend on the timing and character of a distribution made under the other will, particularly for an estate that remains open in both countries at the same time.

Succession in India outside the testamentary framework also has its own appointee for this purpose worth bearing in mind, since Indian banks and depositories generally require a court-issued succession certificate or letters of administration before releasing movable assets to an executor who is not already named on the account, regardless of what either will says about who should receive the asset eventually. An executor who is also the family's main point of contact with Indian banks benefits from understanding this distinction early, since the will alone, without the corresponding Indian court instrument the specific institution asks for, will not by itself unlock an account.

sections.heading: A Practical Checklist for Coordinating the Two Wills
paragraphs: Six points are worth settling before either will is signed, in roughly this order. First, confirm the testator's actual domicile under Sections 6 to 13, rather than assuming it from citizenship or years of residence abroad, since that determines which country's law governs the movable half of the estate and shapes how the foreign will should be drafted. Second, decide which assets go in which will by category, immovable property by location under Section 5, movable property by domicile, rather than by convenience or by which lawyer happens to be drafting which document. Third, draft each will's revocation clause to expressly cover only the assets and jurisdiction that will deals with, and have both lawyers review both clauses together rather than relying on each drafting in isolation.

Fourth, check whether Section 69's automatic revocation on marriage applies to the testator's personal law, and if it does, treat any later marriage as an event requiring an entirely fresh will rather than a mere update. Fifth, choose witnesses and an execution process for each will that matches what the relevant jurisdiction's probate court will actually expect to see, rather than running a single signing ceremony for both documents purely for convenience. None of these steps is individually difficult, but skipping any one of them is exactly how families end up discovering, after a death, that the will they relied on for years did not do what they assumed it did.

A sixth point belongs on the same list even though it is less a drafting question than a scheduling one: calendar a review of both wills every few years, and specifically after any major life event, a move between countries, a marriage, a significant change in assets on either side, rather than treating either document as finished once signed. Cross-border estate plans drift out of alignment quietly, since nothing forces either lawyer to notice that the other jurisdiction's circumstances have changed, and a review that catches a mismatch while the testator is alive and able to execute a correction costs a fraction of what the same mismatch costs a family trying to litigate its way around it after the fact.

sections.heading: What Remains Open
paragraphs: Two points in this area deserve a caveat rather than a confident statement, and a third is worth flagging as a drafting choice rather than a settled legal answer. Which foreign courts' probate grants qualify for the simplified ancillary administration route under Section 228, as opposed to requiring a fresh Indian probate petition, was not confirmed from a primary source in the research for this article, and should be checked against the current statutory position and practice for the specific foreign country involved before an NRI relies on it. While the Kerala High Court's October 2026 ruling upholding Section 69 is recent and directly on point, no report of a further appeal to the Supreme Court was found at the time of writing, so the position should be treated as the current law of the land rather than as a matter beyond any further challenge. And how cleanly a demat shareholding's classification as movable property actually plays out in a contested cross-border estate, given the gap between the registered owner and the beneficial holder this article noted earlier, remains a question commentary has not fully settled, so an NRI with a significant Indian shareholding is better served getting a specific answer for that holding than extending the general domicile rule to it without checking.

conclusion: An NRI's estate is rarely one estate in the eyes of the law, however much it feels like one to the family living through it. Indian immovable property answers to Indian succession rules no matter where the owner was domiciled, foreign movable assets generally answer to the law of the owner's actual domicile, and a will written without that split in mind tends to serve one half of the estate well and leave the other exposed, sometimes fatally, to a revocation clause nobody meant to apply to it.

Two linked wills, each matched to the jurisdiction it covers, each carrying a revocation clause scoped to stay out of the other's way, and each executed with that jurisdiction's own formalities in mind, cost more to set up than a single document but considerably less than the years of delay and litigation that a single will gone wrong tends to produce. The time to find out which trap applies to a given family is before either will is signed, not after the funeral, when the only options left are the ones a probate court is willing to give.

faqs.q: Does an NRI need separate wills for Indian and foreign assets?
faqs.a: Most cross-border estate planning practice recommends two linked wills rather than one, because Indian immovable property is governed by Indian succession law under Section 5 of the Indian Succession Act regardless of the owner's domicile, while foreign assets typically follow the law of the owner's actual domicile. Separate wills let each document match the formalities the relevant court will expect.

faqs.q: Can a will made abroad accidentally cancel an NRI's earlier Indian will?
faqs.a: Yes, and this is the most commonly reported way an Indian will gets destroyed. A standard revocation clause in a later foreign will, phrased broadly enough to revoke all prior wills, is effective under Section 70 of the Indian Succession Act to revoke an earlier Indian will too, unless it is specifically worded to carve out and preserve that Indian will.

faqs.q: Does living abroad for many years change an NRI's legal domicile?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Under Sections 6 to 13 of the Indian Succession Act, a domicile of origin is replaced only by a domicile of choice, which requires both actual residence abroad and a genuine, settled intention to remain there permanently. Residence taken up for employment, however long it continues, does not by itself establish that intention.

faqs.q: Does getting married again automatically cancel an earlier will in India?
faqs.a: It depends on the testator's personal law. Section 69 of the Indian Succession Act automatically revokes a will on the testator's later marriage, but only for Christians, Parsis and Jews. Wills made by Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, Jains and Muslims are not revoked by marriage under this provision, a distinction the Kerala High Court upheld as constitutional on 8 October 2026.

faqs.q: If a will is already probated abroad, does an NRI still need an Indian probate process?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Section 228 of the Indian Succession Act lets an Indian court grant ancillary administration based on an authenticated copy of a will already probated abroad, which can be simpler than a fresh probate petition, but it still requires an application to an Indian court. A foreign probate order does not by itself take effect over Indian immovable property.

faqs.q: Should the same person be the executor for both the Indian and foreign will?
faqs.a: Only if that person can realistically act in both countries without undue delay. It is often more practical to name a different executor in each jurisdiction, someone based in India for the Indian will and someone based in the country of domicile for the foreign will, so that neither half of the estate waits on travel or a power of attorney to make progress.

faqs.q: What is the single most important clause to check in a cross-border will?
faqs.a: The revocation clause in each will. It should state clearly that it revokes only prior wills dealing with the specific jurisdiction and assets that will covers, and that it does not revoke or affect the other will, with both the Indian and the foreign lawyer reviewing both clauses before either document is signed.
